title: Open Question on Circular Drawing Characterisation
statement_text: Is there a theorem that says ``every appropriately connected digraph $G$ contains no thing of type $X$ if and only if $G$ admits a circular drawing''?
context_text: Digraphs are finite and may have loops or parallel edges. A circular drawing of a digraph $G$ is a drawing in the plane without crossings, with the origin in one of the regions, such that every edge subtends a positive angle at the origin (in the clockwise sense); then every directed cycle winds around the origin exactly once. Thomassen proved that if $G$ has no loops or parallel edges, every vertex has in- and out-degree at least two, and there are vertices $a,b$ such that every directed cycle contains $a$ or $b$, then $G$ admits a circular drawing if and only if no directed cycle contains both $a$ and $b$; the question asks for a general theorem of this excluded-structure type. A weighting of $G$ is a function $w:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}$ with total weight $1$ on every directed cycle, and $G$ is weightable if it has one; circular drawings give weightings (take the fraction of a full turn subtended by each edge), so digraphs with circular drawings are weightable. The authors hoped for a converse for sufficiently well-connected digraphs (e.g. strongly 2-connected and weakly 3-connected weightable digraphs), but this is false: they exhibit such a weightable digraph with no circular drawing. Weightable digraphs are known to be exactly those with no subdivided double-cycle, and the authors give a construction of all weightable digraphs (planar ones from circular ones, general ones from planar ones) and a polynomial-time recognition algorithm, but they have still not found the hoped-for characterization of digraphs with circular drawings.
notes: No labelled theorem environment; stated as a motivating open question in the introduction and explicitly left unresolved at the end of the introductory discussion.
